title: Accounts and Brokers
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/0/body: Account names differ between brokers, but the logic is the same: **Standard** has a wider spread and no commission, while **ECN or Raw** has a near-zero spread plus a commission. A **Cent** account shows your balance in cents and is built for trading with very small amounts.
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/0/tip: Before you choose, read the fees and terms for each account on the broker's website.
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/1/pairs/0/mea: The cost is built into the spread
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/1/pairs/2/mea: A live account with very small amounts
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/2/prompt: Reza is a scalper who takes dozens of few-minute trades a day. Which account type is usually cheaper for him?
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/2/options/0: ECN/Raw with a tiny spread and commission
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/2/options/3: No difference; costs don't matter to scalpers
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/2/explanation: A scalper has targets of a few pips and takes lots of trades, so a raw spread plus commission usually costs less overall. Still, always compare your own broker's numbers.
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/3/statement: In a cent account, if you deposit $10, your balance shows as 1,000 units (cents).
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/3/explanation: Each dollar is 100 cents, so $10 = 1,000 cents. These accounts are built for experiencing real money with very little risk.
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/4/prompt: Because of her religious beliefs, Maryam doesn't want to pay or receive interest for holding positions. Which account suits her?
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/4/explanation: A swap-free account has no overnight swap. Some brokers charge an admin fee or a wider spread instead, though, so read the terms.
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/5/body: On a demo, **order fills** can be more ideal than in reality, and you don't feel **fear and greed**. The sign you're ready is **sticking to your plan** over lots of trades, not one big win. After that, start with **small sizes** (or a cent account).
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/6/prompt: Which sign says you're more ready for a live account?
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/6/options/0: You've done dozens of demo trades by the plan
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/6/options/1: One demo trade alone made 50% profit
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/6/options/2: You doubled your demo account in a week
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/6/options/3: A Telegram signal channel said you're ready
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/6/explanation: One big win could be luck. What shows you're ready is following your rules and risk over lots of trades.
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/7/sentence: On ___ accounts the spread is almost raw, but you pay ___ on every lot.
lessons/orders-u3-l1/steps/7/explanation: An ECN or Raw account shows the market's raw spread, and the broker earns its money through a separate commission on every lot.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/title: Choosing a Safe Broker or Exchange
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/0/body: A trustworthy broker works under a **financial regulator**, like the UK's **FCA**, Australia's **ASIC** or Cyprus's **CySEC**, and usually has to keep client money **separate from company money**. Check the license on the **regulator's own official website**; scammers sometimes pose as well-known firms.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/1/prompt: A broker claims to have an FCA license. What's the most reliable way to check?
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/1/options/0: Search for the license on the FCA's own website
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/1/options/1: Spot the FCA logo at the bottom of their site
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/1/options/2: Ask the broker's support for the license number
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/1/explanation: Anyone can fake a logo or a support agent's word. The regulator's official register shows whether the company is really licensed and which website is actually theirs.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/2/body: **Guaranteed profit**, nonstop calls pushing you to deposit more, an **"account manager"** who wants to trade for you, **bonuses** with tough conditions, and excuses when you try to **withdraw** are all warning signs. A trustworthy broker lets you withdraw your money easily.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/2/tip: Deposit a small amount first and make a test withdrawal.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/3/statement: A broker promising "20% guaranteed monthly profit" is showing a serious red flag.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/3/explanation: No market offers fixed, guaranteed profit. That promise is one of the most common scam baits.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/4/title: Crypto exchanges: security and custody risk
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/4/body: With an exchange, look at its **track record**, **security** (like two-factor authentication and withdrawal whitelists) and **proof of reserves**. The **FTX** collapse in 2022 showed that even big exchanges can freeze users' money, so only keep what you need for trading there.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/4/tip: Read the exchange's rules about users' countries; some exchanges have restricted or closed accounts for users in certain countries.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/5/prompt: Which of these lowers the risk of keeping assets on an exchange?
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/5/options/0: Turning on 2FA and keeping only what you trade with
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/5/options/1: One simple password for every site
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/5/options/2: Keeping everything on a brand-new exchange
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/5/options/3: Giving your login details to Telegram support
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/5/explanation: Two-factor authentication stops many hacks, and keeping the rest of your assets off the exchange limits your possible loss from a collapse or hack.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/6/pairs/1/mea: Client money kept apart from company money
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/6/pairs/2/mea: A second code to log in or withdraw
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/6/pairs/3/mea: Showing the assets that back users' funds
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/7/prompt: Put the checklist before depositing with a broker in order.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/7/items/0: Check the license on the regulator's site
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/7/items/1: Read the fees and withdrawal terms
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/7/items/2: Deposit a small amount and test a withdrawal
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/7/items/3: Deposit the rest of your trading capital
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/7/explanation: First make sure the company is real, then read the terms, then test it with a little money. Only send more once a withdrawal goes smoothly.
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/8/prompt: An "account manager" calls and says if you deposit $5,000 today, you'll get a 50% bonus and he'll trade for you. What's the right response?
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/8/options/0: It's a red flag; don't deposit, check the broker
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/8/options/1: It's a limited offer; deposit before it ends
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/8/options/2: Deposit only half to lower the risk
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/8/options/3: Give him your password so he can start sooner
lessons/orders-u3-l2/steps/8/explanation: Time pressure, a big bonus and someone trading for you: that's three red flags at once. A trustworthy broker doesn't pressure you to deposit.
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/0/body: Your **balance** is your account's funds without counting open positions; it usually changes when you close a trade, deposit or withdraw. **Equity** = balance + the floating profit and loss of your open positions, meaning your account's live value.
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/1/prompt: Your balance is $3,000 and you have two open positions: one $200 in profit and one $500 in loss. What's your equity?
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/1/explanation: 3,000 + 200 − 500 = $2,700. Your balance stays at 3,000 as long as these positions are open.
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/2/body: **Margin** is the money locked up to keep your positions open. **Free margin** = equity − margin: the money you have for opening new trades or absorbing more losses.
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/3/statement: When an open position is in a loss, your balance drops right away.
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/3/explanation: A floating loss comes off your equity first. Your balance only changes when you close the position and the loss becomes realized.
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/4/sentence: Equity equals balance plus ___, and free margin equals equity minus ___.
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/4/explanation: Equity is the account's live value (balance + floating), and free margin is the part that isn't locked up (equity − margin).
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/5/prompt: Your balance is $2,000 and you bought 0.5 lots of EUR/USD at 1.0850. The price is now 1.0820. What's your equity?
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/5/explanation: 30 pips against you × $5 (0.5 lots) = $150 floating loss. Equity = 2,000 − 150 = $1,850; your balance is still 2,000.
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/6/title: What does closing a position change?
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/6/body: When you close a position, the floating profit or loss becomes **realized** and is added to or taken from your balance, and its margin is freed up. If free margin gets close to zero, you can't open new trades, and you're near a **margin call**.
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/7/prompt: Same account: $2,000 balance and a position with a $150 floating loss. You close the position. What are your balance and equity now?
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/7/explanation: Closing makes the $150 loss realized, and it comes off your balance. With no open positions left, equity and balance are equal: $1,850.
lessons/orders-u3-l3/steps/8/pairs/1/mea: Funds including floating profit and loss
